Duqueine Team is a French motorsport organization with extensive experience in prototype racing and driver development. Inter Europol Competition is a Polish endurance racing team founded in 2010 and widely recognized by its "Turbo Bakers" nickname. Ultimate is a French family-run racing team founded by former endurance racer Matthieu Lahaye. Known for its determination, hands-on management style, and strong endurance-racing heritage, Ultimate has developed into a consistent presence in the highly competitive LMP3 category.

M Racing is a French endurance racing team headquartered at the Magny-Cours Technopole and supported by touring car legend Yvan Muller. Combining modern facilities, technical expertise, and ambitious long-term goals, M Racing continues to strengthen its position as an emerging force in LMP3 endurance competition.

stories.title: Doohan Survives Silverstone Deluge as Stenzel Storms From the Back
stories.standfirst: A masterstroke on pit strategy handed Jack Doohan LMP2 victory in the Northamptonshire rain, while Matt Stenzel authored an astonishing charge from tenth to take total control of LMP3.
stories.body:
Silverstone has a habit of demanding everything from a racing driver, but the second round of the European Le Mans Series pushed that tariff into overdrive. What began as a high-speed sprint across the sweeping Northamptonshire asphalt devolved into a dramatic afternoon trial against gathering gray clouds and saturated tarmac. When the spray finally settled after 72 relentless minutes, Jack Doohan had outmaneuvered the prototype establishment through sheer tactical precision, while Matt Stenzel turned an unpromising tenth-place grid spot into an utter rout.

With double points on offer in this elongated feature, the championship implications were enormous from the opening seconds, and the fallout has completely reshaped the title landscape heading into the finale.

## Cameron Sets the Pace Before the Deluge

From the drop of the green flag, Dane Cameron looked every bit the driver destined to dominate the day. Launching from third in the #99 AO by TF Oreca, Cameron seized the overall lead into the opening complex, brushing aside pole-sitter **Jack Doohan** in the #24 Nielsen Racing entry and front-row companion Malthe Jakobsen. For the first dozen laps, Cameron set a blistering rhythm, clocking the fastest lap of the race at 1:51.206 and anchoring a tidy two-second cushion over Doohan, Oliver Jarvis, and Paul-Loup Chatin.

Further back, the frantic pace extracted early casualties. Ten laps in, Ian Aguilera suffered a violent impact with the concrete barrier in the #37 CLX Motorsport Oreca, registering a massive 4,241-severity contact that brought his afternoon to an abrupt end.

Cameron pitted for fresh rubber and fuel on lap 12, handing the lead briefly to Doohan before reclaiming it on lap 14 once the pit window cycled through. Yet just as the front-runners settled back into rhythm, the overcast British skies opened up. The circuit rapidly slicked over, forcing teams to confront a pivotal question: pit immediately for wet tyres, or gamble on track position?

## The Lap 32 Pit Lane Calamity

Between laps 19 and 21, the entire prototype field filed in to swap medium slick compounds for grooved rubber. Cameron relinquished the point on lap 19, allowing **Oliver Jarvis** in the #21 United Autosports Oreca to mount a fierce challenge. By lap 25, Jarvis snatched the lead on track, stalking Cameron through the gloom and edging ahead by half a second. For seven laps, Jarvis drove masterfully in the spray, with Cameron and Chatin stacked right behind in a spray-blind three-way fight.

Then came the tactical earthquake. While Doohan in the Nielsen #24 and his teammate James Allen in the #27 car opted to run their wet tyres all the way to the finish after their lap 20 services, the trio of Jarvis, Cameron, and Chatin peeled back into pit lane on lap 32 for an unanticipated second service of fuel and tyres. Jarvis spent a staggering 106 seconds stationary; Cameron lost 105 seconds; Chatin was held for 104.

That tactical miscalculation handed the race on a silver platter to **Jack Doohan**. Sweeping past the pit wall with two laps remaining, Doohan cruised across the line to take a 27.795-second victory over Jarvis, with Cameron crossing 33.145 seconds adrift in third and Chatin just 0.256 seconds behind Cameron in fourth. James Allen completed a sterling recovery drive from 21st on the grid to finish fifth, giving Nielsen Racing a massive haul of points.

Doohan's triumph vaulted him straight to the summit of the LMP2 standings with 69 points, putting him 21 points clear of Allen (48), with Cameron (47) and Jarvis (46) trailing closely behind.

## Stenzel Carves Through the Field

If the LMP2 contest turned on pit lane strategy, the LMP3 category was decided by sheer, unadulterated speed. Starting dead last in tenth after a difficult qualifying run, **Matt Stenzel** faced a daunting task in the #13 Inter Europol Competition Ligier JS P325. Ahead of him, pole-sitter Fabien Michal bolted away in the #85 R-ace GP Duqueine, eager to repeat his Fuji front-running form.

Stenzel did not wait for the race to come to him. Making bold, decisive moves through heavy multi-class traffic, Stenzel dispatched car after car: ninth on lap one, eighth on lap two, sixth on lap three, and fifth by lap four. By lap seven, he had dispatched Matthew Richard Bell for third, and on lap eight, he blew past Sebastian Gravlund into second.

Michal held a four-second lead, but Stenzel chewed it up within four laps. By lap 12, the yellow-and-green Ligier was glued to Michal's rear bumper, trailing by just four-tenths of a second. On lap 13, Stenzel made his move, diving past the Duqueine to take the class lead. Though the two traded the point across pit stops on laps 14 through 18, Stenzel's racecraft remained unshakeable even as he weathered hard rubbing with LMP2 traffic—surviving heavy hits with Sebastian Priaulx and Scott Huffaker along the way.

## The Rain Masterclass

When the heavens fully opened, Stenzel transformed an engaging duel into a procession. Pitting for wet tyres on lap 19, he emerged seven seconds behind Michal. By lap 23, Stenzel caught and passed the Frenchman on track, immediately checking out into a league of his own.

Stenzel’s wet-weather pace was nothing short of devastating. While Michal and Gravlund wrestled their machines through laps in the 2:30 bracket, Stenzel carved through the puddles with a typical wet lap of 2:20.260—matching the times of several LMP2 contenders. He posted the LMP3 fastest lap of 1:56.615 and maintained an exceptional consistency score of 10.736 seconds, far cleaner than the class average of 14.130. A single track limit point collected during his charge was the only minor smudge on an otherwise flawless afternoon.

By the time the checkered flag waved on lap 33, Stenzel took the victory by an astonishing 97.758 seconds over Michal, with Gravlund claiming the final step on the podium nearly two minutes behind. Bell trailed home in fourth, while Grégory de Sybourg crossed a lap down in fifth.

With 51 points pocketed for the victory, Stenzel extends his LMP3 championship lead to 78 points, establishing a formidable 21-point cushion over Michal (57) and Gravlund (36). Everything now hinges on the final showdown at the Festival of Portimão at Autódromo Internacional do Algarve, where the inaugural Speed Challengers crowns will finally be decided.

stories.title: Allen Commands the Mountain as Stenzel Survives Fuji Carnage
stories.standfirst: James Allen swept every point on offer in LMP2 while Matt Stenzel weathered an early stop and a late prototype collision to claim a dramatic LMP3 opener at Fuji.
stories.body:
The shadow of Mount Fuji provided a serene backdrop for the curtain-raiser of the 2026 Speed Challengers campaign, but the 45-minute sprint across the tarmac of Fuji International Speedway was anything but peaceful. When the green flag unfurled over the 33-car grid under clear morning skies, it ignited an unrelenting contest across two fiercely competitive prototype classes. With the championship offering a escalating points scale across its three rounds, setting an early marker in Japan was vital. Two drivers did exactly that—one through cold, surgical perfection at the front of the field, and the other through sheer tenacity amidst late-race chaos.

## Allen Leads a Nielsen Masterclass

From the moment qualifying concluded, Nielsen Racing looked to have unlocked something special around the 4.56-kilometer circuit. **James Allen** had converted that inherent pace into pole position by less than a tenth of a second over AO by TF’s **Dane Cameron**, with teammate **Jack Doohan** lurking in third. When the lights went out, Allen drove off the line with clean authority, sweeping into Turn 1 to secure an immediate advantage he would refuse to surrender for the entirety of the 28-lap duration.

Behind Allen, the LMP2 front-runners ran locked in formation, separated by fractions of a second. Cameron spent the opening sixteen laps glued to Allen's rear wing, never trailing by more than eight-tenths of a second, while Doohan hounded them both from third. Behind them, TDS Racing’s **Scott Huffaker** kept the pressure on in fourth, keeping the leading trio honest. The decisive strategic moment arrived on lap 17, when the entire LMP2 field peeled into the pit lane in unison for mandatory splash-and-dash fuel stops. 

While Allen enjoyed a seamless 62-second stationary service to emerge still in the lead, Nielsen’s crew pulled off an inspired turnaround on the sister car. Doohan cleared Cameron in the lane as Cameron's crew clocked a 64-second stop, vaulting the #24 Oreca into second. Doohan then unleashed blistering pace on his scrubbed mediums, hunting down Allen over the closing laps. By lap 24, the gap between the two Nielsen prototypes had evaporated to absolute zero as they navigated backmarker traffic through Sector 3. Allen held his nerve, carving through the slower classes with razor-thin precision to fend off Doohan by a scant 0.629 seconds at the stripe, with Cameron finishing third just 1.386 seconds adrift.

## Stenzel's Opening Lap Coup

While Allen executed a textbook lights-to-flag victory in LMP2, the LMP3 battle unfolded with unbridled drama. Pole-sitter **Fabien Michal** led the pack into Turn 1 aboard the solitary R-ace GP Duqueine D09, flanked by the nine-car Ligier armada. Yet the real story of the start was **Matt Stenzel**. Starting fourth on the grid in the #13 Inter Europol Competition Ligier JS P325, Stenzel produced a sensational opening tour, aggressively carving past **Sebastian Gravlund**, **Grégory de Sybourg**, and Michal before the first lap was out.

Once in clean air, Stenzel showed pace that shocked the class. He laid down an astonishing lap of 1:38.664—more than two seconds faster than Michal’s best effort of 1:40.853—and built an 8.4-second lead by lap 13. While de Sybourg and DKR Engineering’s **Wyatt Brichacek** squabbled over third, Michal kept his head, relying on metronomic consistency in the Duqueine to keep the flying Polish entry within sight.

## Strategy Inverts the Order

With tire wear virtually negligible over the 45-minute sprint, the race hinged on fuel timing. Stenzel and Inter Europol chose to blink early, diving into pit lane at the end of lap 15. The 53-second stop dropped the #13 car all the way to tenth in class, momentarily handing the lead back to Michal. The French driver responded with a succession of steady laps in the low 1:41s, extending his stint to lap 22 before making his own stop. De Sybourg pushed one lap further, leading lap 23 before ducking in for fuel.

When the pit cycle finally concluded on lap 24, Stenzel’s aggressive undercut paid massive dividends. As de Sybourg rejoined in third and Michal merged back onto the track, Stenzel came howling down the front straight, sweeping past to reclaim the LMP3 lead with a comfortable cushion. Yet the sprint was far from decided, as the closing minutes threatened to undo everything Stenzel had built.

## Heartbreak Averted at the Wire

At minute 42, just as the leading LMP2 machines began their final laps, disaster nearly struck for the LMP3 leader. Fighting through dense multi-class traffic, Stenzel made heavy contact with the LMP2 Oreca of **Paul-Loup Chatin**, an enormous hit registering a 3,075 severity score that sent shockwaves through both machines. Before Stenzel could fully gather the Ligier, secondary impacts with the barriers followed in rapid succession. 

Miraculously, the #13 machine retained its steering and structural integrity, though the incident sheared precious seconds from Stenzel's lead. Michal sensed blood and charged, trimming the margin down to just a single second on lap 25. Having accumulated four track limit warnings over the course of the sprint, Stenzel had to walk a technical tightrope on damaged rhythm. But the Inter Europol driver gathered himself brilliantly over the final two laps, stabilizing the gap to cross the line 2.970 seconds ahead of Michal. De Sybourg rounded out the podium a distant 24.847 seconds behind, having successfully defended third from Brichacek.

## The Title Picture Takes Shape

With the opening round in the books, the championship tables reflect a pair of commanding early leaders. In LMP2, James Allen stands atop the standings with a maximum haul of 28 points, having swept pole position, the race victory, fastest lap, and all 28 laps led. Jack Doohan sits second with 18 points, anchoring a dominant 46-point haul for Nielsen Racing, while Dane Cameron holds third with 15 points.

In LMP3, Matt Stenzel matches that authority, leading the standings with 27 points after capturing the victory, the bonus point for fastest lap, and leading 18 laps. Michal's pole position and runner-up finish net him 19 points, keeping R-ace GP well within striking distance, while de Sybourg leaves Japan with 15.

The Speed Challengers season now heads west to the historic asphalt of the British Grand Prix at Silverstone Circuit. With Round 2 scheduled as a 72-minute long endurance contest offering a massive 50 points to the winner, the stakes will double under the looming threat of traditional British rain.

stories.title: Three Rounds, No Margin: Inside the Fast and Furious ELMS Season 2 Campaign
stories.standfirst: A compressed three-race calendar across three iconic circuits sets the stage for an explosive LMP2 and LMP3 championship brawl.
stories.body:
The engines are quiet for now, resting under the awnings and behind pit garage doors, but the tension heading into Season 2 of the Speed Series is palpable. A three-round European Le Mans Series sprint-to-endurance journey offers nowhere to hide and zero room for early-season missteps. With a calendar that scales from an all-out 45-minute sprint to a grueling 72-minute wet-weather marathon and culminates in a rollercoaster Algarve finale, this championship demands immediate perfection from both the headline LMP2 heavyweights and the relentless junior prototypes of LMP3.

Every point will feel magnified under this structure. The opener awards 25 points for victory, but Round 2 at Silverstone blows the doors open as a Long format race offering an immense 50-point haul to the winner, before Portimão wraps up the fight with a 38-point Medium distance finale. Throw in single bonus markers for pole position, fastest lap, and most laps led in every race, and the math becomes razor-sharp: one stumble, and your championship aspirations are done before midsummer.

## The Crucible: Three Circuits, Three Entirely Different Tests

Opening the campaign under the shadow of Mount Fuji, Round 1 takes the paddock to Japan for the Rising Sun Race Weekend. Running the fearsome Fuji Classic layout without the fiddly modern final-sector chicane, the 45-minute sprint promises pure slipstreaming bedlam. Drivers will thunder down the endless 1.5-kilometer front straight before braking brutally into the tight Turn 1 hairpin, then carry frightening momentum through the long sweeping rights of 100R and 300R. It is a circuit made for aerodynamic bravery and slipstream chess, contested under bright morning skies.

If Fuji tests raw top-end speed, Round 2 drops the field directly into endurance purgatory. The British Grand Prix at Silverstone expands the race length to 72 minutes and introduces the great equalizer: forecasted rain. Silverstone in the wet is legendary for separating the contenders from the pretenders. Navigating Maggotts, Becketts, and Chapel on a slick surface with standing water and 50 points on the line will require unflinching nerve and surgeon-like car control. Traffic management between the top-class Orecas and the chasing LMP3 pack through Copse and Stowe will be white-knuckle stuff.

Then comes the decider: the Festival of Portimão at the Autódromo Internacional do Algarve. Sixty minutes around Portugal’s undulating roller coaster, where blind crests, plunging downhill braking zones, and technical off-camber sweepers punish exhausted tires. By the time the grid rolls into the Algarve sun, the championship picture will be down to a select few with everything left to prove.

## LMP2: World-Class Powerhouses on a Collision Course

Eleven Oreca 07-Gibsons make up the premier class, and the grid reads like an endurance racing directory of championship caliber. Proton Competition enters the #9 Oreca featuring sports car ace **Mike Rockenfeller** alongside **Sebastian Priaulx** and **Jonas Ried**, a trio blessed with world-class discipline and pedigree. But they will face immediate resistance from United Autosports, who arrive with **Ben Hanley**, **Grégoire Saucy**, and **Garett Grist Peebles** in the #22 machine—a lineup built on blistering single-lap pace and tactical aggression.

IDEC Sport brings a formidable two-car assault with the #18 steered by **Jamie Chadwick**, **Vanina Ickx Rinicella**, and **Laurents Hörr**, accompanied by the sister #28 piloted by proven winners **Job van Uitert** and **Paul-Loup Chatin** alongside **Paul Lafargue**. Over at Inter Europol Competition, their top-tier effort is doubled up with the dangerous #34 entry of **Bijoy Garg** and **Reshad de Gerus**, paired with the seasoned trio of **Jakub Śmiechowski**, **Tom Dillmann**, and **Nick Yelloly** in the #43.

Throw in Algarve Pro Racing’s #25—anchored by **Tristan Vautier** and **Jake Hughes**—and the sheer depth of Nielsen Racing’s #24 boasting **Jack Doohan** and **Roy Nissany**, and LMP2 looks primed for an absolute dogfight from the first green flag in Japan.

## Stenzel and the LMP3 Hornet’s Nest

The LMP3 division will be no less ferocious. Ten prototypes pack the entry list, dominated by nine snarling Ligier JS P325s against a lone, defiant Duqueine D09 entered by R-ace GP for **Fabien Michal**, **Pierre-Alexandre Provost**, and **Hugo Schwarze**. 

Sitting squarely in the spotlight of this junior prototype warfare is **Matt Stenzel**, strapping into the iconic yellow-and-green livery of Inter Europol Competition’s #13 Ligier JS P325 alongside **Alexander Bukhantsov**, **Chun-Ting Chou**, and **Henry Cubides Olarte**. For Stenzel, the stakes could not be clearer. In a sprint-heavy schedule where qualifying sets the tone and race craft in multi-class traffic dictates survival, Stenzel will have to extract maximum pace while negotiating faster LMP2 traffic flashing into his mirrors.

The competition in LMP3 is merciless. DKR Engineering brings their serial-winning prototype prowess with the #4 Ligier driven by **Wyatt Brichacek**, **Romain Favre**, and **Antti Rammo**. Eurointernational’s #11, led by prototype veteran **Matthew Richard Bell**, will provide a stern benchmark on every circuit, while Team Virage (#8) and Racing Spirit of Leman (#31) bring proven race-winning operations to the grid.

For Stenzel and Inter Europol, surviving the high-speed chaos of Fuji’s slipstream wars will be vital to establish momentum. If they can escape Round 1 with a solid points haul, the grueling wet weather of Silverstone’s 72-minute double-points showdown could turn into their greatest opportunity—or their most unforgiving trap.

## The Countdown Begins

With 90 percent AI competition intensity dialed in and three radically divergent tracks awaiting, the opening lap at Fuji Classic cannot arrive soon enough. Three rounds sound brief on paper, but across 177 minutes of high-stakes prototype racing, reputations will be cemented and heartbreaks will be suffered.

The engines will fire soon under the morning sky in Oyama. Let the battle begin.
